opus-5.5.text:
I think Kaiming's influence is quite unusual, and it isn't only about the number of famous papers. It's more about a *taste*, a way of doing research that a lot of people in our field have absorbed, sometimes without realizing where it came from.

The first thing I'd point to is simplicity. If you look at ResNet, the core idea is almost embarrassingly simple: add a shortcut connection so the network learns a residual. Many people could have written that down. But Kaiming has a very strong belief that the right idea should be simple, and that if your method needs ten tricks to work, you probably haven't found the real thing yet. That standard of "strip it down until only the essential part is left" really shaped how a whole generation thinks about architecture and method design.

The second thing is rigor and honesty in experiments. When I worked with Kaiming, it was striking how much time went into ablations, into really understanding *why* something works, not just showing that it beats a baseline. Their papers read almost like careful scientific reports. Every claim is backed by a controlled experiment, and the writing is very clean. People trust a Kaiming paper because they know the conclusions have been stress-tested. That kind of credibility is rare, and it gives the work a long life.

Third, there's a kind of patience and focus. Kaiming doesn't chase every trend or publish a lot of incremental work. They pick a fundamental problem, like optimization of deep networks, detection, or self-supervised learning with MoCo and later MAE, and go deep. Often the work arrives at a moment when the field is confused, and it cuts through that confusion. MAE is a good example: the idea of masking a large fraction of patches and reconstructing them is very simple, but it reframed how people thought about visual pretraining.

And I think on a personal level, as a mentor, the influence comes from example more than instruction. You don't get long lectures. You see how they question a result, how they rewrite a paragraph five times so it says exactly one thing, how they're willing to throw away a direction that isn't clean. For me that was a formative experience. Even now, when I'm working on something, I sometimes ask myself, "Would this pass Kaiming's bar? Is this the simplest version of the idea?" I think many people who've worked with them carry that same voice in their heads. That, to me, is the most distinctive kind of influence a researcher can have.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming He’s influence through simplicity, experimental rigor, focus, and mentorship. It does not say that people around him came to see previously impossible goals as achievable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing people notice about Kaiming is that his work is almost unreasonably simple. ResNet is the obvious example. The idea of a residual connection fits in one sentence, you can draw it on a napkin, and yet it completely changed how deep networks are built. That's not an accident. He has this very deliberate taste for stripping a problem down until only the essential thing is left. A lot of researchers, myself included at times, add complexity because it makes a paper look more sophisticated. Kaiming does the opposite. He removes things until it breaks, and then he puts back exactly one piece.

The second thing is that he's extremely honest with experiments. When we worked together on things like ResNeXt or later on masked autoencoders, the discipline was always the same. Control everything, change one variable, and if the result doesn't support the story, change the story, not the result. He doesn't fall in love with his own hypothesis. I remember being surprised early on by how willing he was to throw away weeks of work if an ablation said it didn't matter.

And then there's the way he picks problems. He tends to go after questions that feel fundamental rather than fashionable. Normalization, depth, how to pretrain in vision, whether vision really needs all the machinery that was accumulating around it. When the whole field was moving toward transformers and a lot of people assumed convolutions were finished, we did ConvNeXt partly because of that mindset: let's actually check instead of assuming. That kind of "wait, is this really true?" attitude is something I absorbed from him.

Finally, I think his influence is as much about style as about any single result. There's a whole generation of researchers who write papers the way he does. Clean baselines, short method sections, big ablation tables, no hand-waving. He showed that you can be enormously influential without being loud. He doesn't dominate a room. He just quietly asks the right question, and a year later everyone is working on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Kaiming’s influence through simplicity, experimental discipline, problem choice, and research style, but does not say that people around him come to see previously impossible goals as achievable.

astra-6.text:
I think Kaiming’s distinctive influence is his taste in problems and his ability to make a complicated question feel simple. It’s not just that he finds a method that works. He often identifies the underlying obstacle and gives people a very clear way to think about it.

That kind of clarity is difficult to achieve. A simple idea can look obvious after someone has explained it, but getting there requires knowing which details matter and which ones you can remove. To me, that’s a very powerful research quality.

And the influence goes beyond any individual result. It sets a standard: Can you ask a more fundamental question? Can you explain why your approach works? Can other researchers build on it? I think that’s what makes his work so influential—it changes how people approach their own problems.

r001.rationale: The response says Kaiming’s clarity and research standards influence how others approach problems, but does not say that people around him perceive previously impossible goals as achievable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Kaiming’s distinctive influence is his ability to find a very simple idea inside a complicated problem. A lot of research adds components: you have a problem, you add a module, and then another module. His instinct seems to be to ask, “What is the essential obstacle here? Can we change the formulation so that the problem becomes easier?” That way of thinking is very powerful.

And simplicity doesn’t mean the work is easy. Often you need a very deep understanding to know what you can remove, which experiment will actually answer the question, and whether a result supports the explanation you’re giving. What I admire is that combination of conceptual clarity and experimental rigor.

So his influence goes beyond individual papers. He gives people a model of what good research can look like: identify a fundamental question, investigate it carefully, and arrive at something that feels almost obvious afterward. Getting to that “obvious” idea is the difficult part.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming’s influence as modeling clear, rigorous research, but does not say he makes people around him see previously impossible goals as achievable.
